Some examples include a GMC Hummer being charged by the 350-kW EVSE (collected as part of the Next- Generation Profiles [NextGen Profiles] project [11]) and a Hyundai Ioniq 5 being charged by a 25-kW EVSE. As expected, power draw of the Hummer is much higher and varies more than the Ioniq [11]. This is due in part to the power limitation of the 25-kW EVSE, so the Ioniq draws a constant power over a large span of the SOC range. In general, power profile curves like those shown in Figure 1 are a function of session-specific conditions like ambient temperature and battery initial SOC. They are also a function of hardware-specific parameters, like EV and EVSE model, and complex active control decisions made by the EV’s battery management system and EVSE. 3 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Charge demand curve examples 2.3 Site Optimization Solutions A critical component to coordinate EV charging load flexibility and site DER assets is the development of an SCM objective function. This SCM objective function must monitor all EV charging, building loads, and DER to optimize sitewide net demand. The SCM must leverage PV generation, charge or discharge the energy storage system, and manage EV charging power to maintain net demand within sitewide capacity limits to mitigate the need for costly upgrades. There are a few system requirements that must be supported to enable this SCM. Depending on the site’s capabilities, namely the presence of detailed fleet operation schedules, two control strategies are described in this report: “Gold” and “Platinum” controls. Figure 2. Sitewide net load overview 4 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 2.3.1 Gold Control The Gold SCM uses a feedback control framework, making decisions solely based on information received from the hardware. Additionally, each piece of equipment is considered separately—a limitation usually associated with feedback or heuristic rules—as opposed to predictive control strategies, creating challenges for optimizing the whole-site performance. Each of the main parts of the control framework is described next. The main control subtasks are executed in the following order: • Track fleet and facility operations using MQTT messages: EVSE power and SOC, BESS power and SOC, and solar and building power. • EV-EVSE assignment: Identify incoming EVs and assign them to EVSE. • EVSE curtailment: Calculate EVSE power curtailment set points assuming BESS can be discharged at maximum power. • BESS dispatch: Calculate BESS power set point based on current measurements. • Update BESS and EVSE set points by sending MQTT messages.
